questions.q: You read ada.describe, and ada has no own property called describe. What does JavaScript do?
questions.explain: Reads walk the prototype chain. Only when the chain ends at null without a match is the result undefined.
options: Looks at ada's prototype, then that object's prototype, and so on, until it finds describe or reaches null
Searches every object in the program for a property with that name

questions.q: describe is found on ada's grand-prototype, and called as ada.describe(). What is this inside it?
questions.explain: Where a method is found and how it is called are separate questions. The call ada.describe() sets this to ada, so one shared method works on every object that inherits it.
options: ada, the object the method was called on

questions.q: defaults has currency: "NGN", and ada = Object.create(defaults). What does ada.currency = "USD" do?
questions.explain: Reads walk the chain; ordinary writes do not. They create or change an own property on the object you assign to.
options: Creates an own currency on ada that shadows the inherited one; defaults is unchanged
Throws, because inherited properties are read-only

questions.q: A prototype has a setter set pin(value) { … }. What does ada.pin = "1234" do on an object that inherits from it?
questions.explain: A setter found on the chain intercepts the assignment. That is how one setter on a class prototype validates writes for every instance.
options: Creates an own data property pin on ada
Calls the inherited setter with this set to ada; no own pin is created
Replaces the setter on the prototype
Throws, because setters cannot be inherited

questions.q: A prototype has a non-writable property bank. In strict mode, what happens with ada.bank = "Other", where ada has no own bank?
questions.explain: An inherited read-only data property stops assignment, even though the write would go to ada. Object.defineProperty(ada, "bank", …) could still add an own one.
options: A TypeError: an inherited read-only property blocks plain assignment
It works only if ada is frozen

questions.q: ada has an own currency that shadows "NGN" on its prototype. After delete ada.currency, what is ada.currency?
questions.explain: delete only removes own properties. The prototype's property was never touched, so it is visible again.
options: "NGN", the inherited value shows through again
The prototype's property is deleted too, so undefined

questions.q: A prototype has items: [] and a method add(sku) { this.items.push(sku); }. Why do all carts share one list?
questions.explain: Only assignment creates own properties. Keep data on instances (set it in the constructor) and put only methods and constants on prototypes.
options: Arrays are always shared in JavaScript
this.items is a read that finds the one array on the prototype, and push changes that array; nothing is ever written to the cart itself
push copies the array onto every object

questions.q: What is at the end of the prototype chain of a normal object literal?
questions.explain: Object.prototype provides toString, hasOwnProperty and friends. Its [[Prototype]] is null, which ends every lookup.

questions.q: Why is Object.hasOwn(obj, key) safer than obj.hasOwnProperty(key)?
questions.explain: Methods found through the chain can be absent or replaced. A static function on Object does not depend on the object's chain at all.
options: hasOwnProperty is itself inherited: it is missing on null-prototype objects and can be shadowed by a data field with that name; Object.hasOwn is a static function that always works

questions.q: Why should you avoid Object.setPrototypeOf on objects in code that runs for every request?
questions.explain: Set the prototype when the object is created (Object.create, new, class). Linking prototypes once at start-up, as inherit does, is fine.
options: It deletes the object's own properties
Engines optimise objects by their shape and prototype; changing the prototype later makes code that uses the object slower
It changes the prototype of every object

questions.q: What is obj.__proto__?
questions.explain: Use Object.getPrototypeOf and Object.create instead. The __proto__ accessor is also what prototype pollution attacks reach through.
options: An own property every object is created with
An old getter/setter on Object.prototype that reads or changes the prototype link; legacy, and missing on objects that do not inherit from Object.prototype

questions.q: Which list describes what new Fn(args) does, in order?
questions.explain: Methods are not copied; the new object is linked to Fn.prototype and finds them by lookup. A returned object replaces the new one; a returned primitive is ignored.
options: Call Fn, copy its return value, link it to Fn.prototype
Create an object linked to Fn.prototype; call Fn with it as this; return Fn's result if that is an object, otherwise the new object
Copy every method of Fn.prototype into a new object, then call Fn
Create an object linked to Fn itself, then call Fn.prototype

questions.q: A constructor function ends with return { error: "not allowed" } in one branch. What does new give in that branch?
questions.explain: Step 3 of new: an object returned from the constructor replaces the new object. It is legal and surprising, so avoid it.
options: The new object, with an error property added
The returned plain object, which is not linked to the constructor's prototype

questions.q: For a constructor function Order, which statement is true?
questions.explain: The prototype property is only used by new. The function itself inherits call, apply and bind from Function.prototype.
options: Order.prototype is the prototype of the function Order
Order.prototype becomes the prototype of instances; the function's own prototype is Function.prototype

questions.q: What happens with new ((owner) => { this.owner = owner; })("Ada")?
questions.explain: Arrows (and methods written with method syntax) cannot be used with new. Use a class or a function declaration for constructors.
options: It throws a TypeError: arrow functions are not constructors and have no prototype property

questions.q: Old code writes SavingsAccount.prototype = Object.create(Account.prototype). Why does it usually follow with SavingsAccount.prototype.constructor = SavingsAccount?
questions.explain: The new prototype object inherits constructor from Account.prototype. instanceof would still work (it checks the chain), but ada.constructor and anything that uses it would be wrong.
options: The replaced prototype object lost its constructor property, so instances would report Account as their constructor
It is needed for instanceof to work

questions.q: In an old-style child constructor, what does Account.call(this, owner, balanceKobo) correspond to in a class?
questions.explain: Both run the parent's setup code on the new object, so it gets the parent's own properties. The prototype link is the separate job of extends.

questions.q: What does obj instanceof Fn actually check?
questions.explain: It only walks the chain. An object from Object.create(Fn.prototype) passes without ever running Fn, and replacing Fn.prototype later makes old instances fail.
options: Whether obj was created by calling new Fn
Whether obj has all the properties that Fn sets
Whether Fn.prototype appears anywhere on obj's prototype chain

questions.q: An array created inside an iframe fails value instanceof Array in the parent page. What should you use instead?
questions.explain: Each frame has its own Array.prototype, so instanceof compares against the wrong one. Array.isArray checks the kind of object directly and works across frames. (typeof an array is "object".)

questions.q: Why does for...in over an instance of an old constructor function list its methods, while the same loop over a class instance does not?
questions.explain: for...in lists enumerable properties, own and inherited. Class syntax defines methods with enumerable: false, so only data shows up.
options: Methods assigned with Fn.prototype.m = function… are enumerable; class methods are defined as non-enumerable
for...in does not work on class instances

questions.q: class SavingsAccount extends Account {} creates which prototype links?
questions.explain: The second link is why SavingsAccount.fromJSON works when fromJSON is a static method of Account.
options: SavingsAccount.prototype → Account.prototype (instances inherit methods) and SavingsAccount → Account (static members are inherited)
It copies all of Account's methods into SavingsAccount

questions.q: A naive deep merge copies JSON.parse('{"__proto__":{"isAdmin":true}}') into {}. Why does every object now have isAdmin: true?
questions.explain: JSON.parse makes "__proto__" an ordinary own key. The damage happens when a merge uses it as a property name on a normal target.
options: Reading target["__proto__"] goes through the inherited accessor and returns Object.prototype; the merge then writes isAdmin onto it, and every ordinary object inherits it
The merge adds isAdmin to each object one by one
It does not; isAdmin only appears on the merged object

questions.q: Which is not an effective defence against prototype pollution?
questions.explain: Every parsed JSON object is an instanceof Object, including the malicious one. The other three remove the dangerous keys or the path to Object.prototype.
options: Skipping the keys __proto__, constructor and prototype when copying outside data
Using Object.create(null) or a Map for data keyed by user input
Validating the body against a schema and copying only expected fields

questions.q: A teammate adds Array.prototype.sum = function () { … } so every array has sum(). What is the main problem?
questions.explain: Built-in prototypes are shared by all code. Write a normal function, sum(array), instead of extending them.
options: It only works for arrays created afterwards
It changes every array in the process, including inside libraries, and a future JavaScript version may add a built-in method with the same name and different behaviour

questions.explain: describe is found two levels up, but this is ada. this.kind is then looked up from ada and found on savings first. isPrototypeOf checks the whole chain.

questions.explain: Both carts read the single array on the prototype and push into it. Neither cart ever gets an own items.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The first delete removes the own shadow, so the inherited value shows. The second delete finds no own property and does nothing: it never touches the prototype.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A returned primitive is ignored, so a is the new object. A returned object replaces the new object, so b is the plain { y: 2 }, which is not linked to B.prototype.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: instanceof only checks the chain, and Order.prototype is on it. The constructor never ran, so there is no id.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: old is still linked to the original prototype object, which is no longer Invoice.prototype. Only objects created after the replacement are linked to the new one.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: for...in lists enumerable properties along the whole chain. The assigned prototype method is enumerable; the class method is not.

questions.explain: extends links the classes themselves, so the static method is found on Account. It is called on SavingsAccount, so this.name is "SavingsAccount".
options: TypeError: SavingsAccount.bank is not a function

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A null-prototype object has an empty chain: no inherited toString, and Object.prototype is not on its chain, so instanceof Object is false.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Order.prototype is the prototype of instances. The function Order itself inherits from Function.prototype.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: owner is own; describe is inherited from Account.prototype and toString from Object.prototype. in follows the chain; Object.hasOwn does not.

questions.q: This old-style inheritance forgets one line. What does this print?
questions.explain: The replacement prototype has no own constructor, so s.constructor is found on Account.prototype. instanceof still works, because it only checks the chain.

questions.q: Using only Object.create (no classes, no new), make ada inherit describe from accountMethods, with own properties owner: "Ada" and balanceKobo: 250000.
questions.explain: Object.create(accountMethods) links the new object to the methods object. The data goes on ada itself; the method is found by lookup.

questions.q: Write construct(Fn, ...args) that does what new Fn(...args) does: link a new object to Fn.prototype, call Fn with it as this, and return the constructor's result if it is an object (not null), otherwise the new object.
questions.explain: These are the four steps of new: create with the right prototype, call with it as this, and choose which object to return.

questions.q: Write isInstance(obj, Fn) that gives the same answers as obj instanceof Fn by walking the prototype chain with Object.getPrototypeOf. Primitives and null return false.
questions.explain: Checking constructor fails for subclasses and null-prototype objects. instanceof walks the whole chain looking for Fn.prototype, and treats primitives as not instances.
questions.expected: true true false true false false

questions.q: Write a constructor function Invoice(id, totalKobo) and put a describe() method on Invoice.prototype, so both invoices share one method.
questions.explain: The constructor sets the data on each new object; the method lives once on the prototype, so both invoices find the same function.

questions.q: Link SavingsAccount to Account the pre-class way: call the parent constructor, link the prototypes with Object.create, and restore constructor.
questions.explain: Account.call(this, owner) plays the role of super(owner); Object.create(Account.prototype) is the prototype half of extends; restoring constructor fixes what replacing the prototype object threw away.

questions.q: All carts share one items array. Fix it so each cart has its own array, while add stays on the prototype.
questions.explain: Data belongs on the instance, created in the constructor. Methods belong on the prototype, where they are shared.

questions.q: Write ownAndInherited(obj) that returns { own, inherited }: arrays of the property names found on the object itself and on each prototype above it (use Object.getOwnPropertyNames), stopping before Object.prototype. Skip constructor.
questions.explain: Class methods are non-enumerable, so Object.keys on the prototypes would miss them; Object.getOwnPropertyNames lists every string key. The walk goes from the nearest prototype outwards.

questions.q: This merge lets a request body pollute Object.prototype. Make it skip the keys __proto__, constructor and prototype, and iterate with Object.keys.
questions.explain: Skipping the three names closes both routes to Object.prototype (__proto__ directly, and constructor.prototype). The finally removes any pollution so the starter does not break later runs.
